en: The Sutra on the Twelve Dhūtas Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Khotan during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Together with a community of eight thousand bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas, all wearing robes and carrying alms bowls, they went on their rounds to beg for food.
Having finished eating, they proceeded to a forest hermitage (āraṇya) and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled serenely.
Then, the Elder Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Since time immemorial, I have never seen a Buddha smile without cause.
I pray that you will look upon us with compassion and grant us an explanation.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Beholding this araṇya dwelling, all the Buddhas of the ten directions praise it; immeasurable merits arise from it. Those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas obtain the śrāvaka-yāna;

those seeking the pratyekabuddha-yāna obtain the pratyekabuddha-yāna; and those seeking the Mahāyāna swiftly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Since I now dwell here, I am filled with joy!"

At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha had said, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The benefits of this araṇya site are vast and profound; it enables sentient beings to rely upon it for study and practice, thereby accomplishing the paths of the three vehicles.
We only pray, World-Honored One, that you will reveal to us the Dharma of the araṇya.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well!
I shall briefly explain its meaning for you."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“A forest-dwelling bhikṣu remains far removed from the two attachments; with body and mind pure, he practices the dhūta ascetic virtues.
There are twelve matters for one who practices these dharmas:”
First, dwelling in an araṇya;
second, constantly practicing alms-gathering;
third, begging for food in successive order.
Fourth, the practice of eating only one meal a day;
fifth, moderation in the quantity of food consumed;
sixth, not drinking any liquids after midday.
Seventh, wearing tattered rag-robes;
eighth, possessing only the three robes;
ninth, dwelling among burial mounds;
Tenth, dwelling under a tree;
eleventh, sitting in the open air;
twelfth, sitting only and not lying down.
"First, when an araṇya bhikṣu practices the dhūta austerities, he should form this thought:

'I am now in this secluded place; for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I relinquish body, life, and wealth to cultivate the three firm dharmas. When I die, I shall die like a discarded corpse, without giving rise to any lingering attachment.'"
When one reaches a time of illness and suffering when another person is needed, one should form this thought:

"I have now gone forth from home for the sake of the Dharma alone; the Dharma is my companion. If I diligently practice the Dharma, that itself is my protection and refuge. This is the dharma of the araṇya-dweller.

The practitioner originally left home because domestic life is full of afflictions; having abandoned parents, wife, and children to leave the household and practice the Way, they may still develop attachments toward their teachers, disciples, and fellow students, causing the mind to become once again disturbed and distracted. For this reason, one adopts the dharma of the araṇya, so that the body remains far removed from clamor and dwells in seclusion.
Regarding "physical seclusion": it means being far removed from the clamor of crowds. Whether at a cattle-pasture or elsewhere, one should stay at least three *li* away; the further, the better.
Once physical seclusion has been attained, one must also cause the mind to be secluded from the five desires and the five hindrances.
The dharma for an araṇya bhikṣu should be thus:

"Second, when wishing to enter a village to beg for food, one should restrain the six sense faculties so that they do not become attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; furthermore, one should not discriminate between the marks of male and female, and whether food is obtained or not, the mind should remain equanimous, giving rise to neither increase nor decrease toward what is good or bad."
When not receiving food, one should reflect:

"Even when Śākyamuni Tathāgata renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to leave home and attain the Way, he encountered instances where he received nothing while entering villages to beg for alms; how much more so for a person like me, who lacks merit and has meager virtue—how could I possibly receive anything?"
This is the practice for one who begs for food.
Whether receiving an invitation to eat or partaking in a communal meal of the Sangha, these give rise to the causes and conditions for the outflows (āsrava). Why is this so?
When one who has accepted an invitation to eat receives food, they think:
"I have obtained this because I am a person of merit and virtue.
If they do not receive food, they harbor resentment toward the host:
"He lacks discernment; he requests those who should not be requested and does not request those who should be requested.
Or, being self-contemptuous, distressed, and self-reproachful, he gives rise to sorrow and suffering. Such dharmas of craving can obstruct the Path.

Regarding those who eat with the Sangha: when entering among the assembly, one should follow the rules of the community; yet if one adjudicates disputes, expels individuals, manages monastic affairs, or assigns tasks and errands, the mind will become distracted, hindering and obstructing the practice of the Path.
Because there are such disturbances and afflictions as these, one should practice the method of constant alms-seeking.

"Third, the dhūta bhikṣu does not become attached to forms and does not disparage sentient beings; with a mind of equal compassion, he makes no distinction between the poor and the wealthy, and therefore practices the method of constant sequential alms-seeking."
"Fourth, one should reflect thus:
'If even seeking a single meal now creates many obstacles for me, how much more so for morning meals, midday meals, and afternoon meals? "

If one does not diminish [worldly concerns], then one loses half the merit of the day and cannot practice the Way with a single mind; for the sake of the Buddha-Dharma and for the sake of practicing the Way, one should not act for the sake of body or life, like tending horses or pigs.
"Therefore, one should sever the practice of eating repeatedly and should instead observe the rule of eating only once a day.
Fifth, when obtaining food for a single meal, one should form this thought:
'If I now see a sentient being who is parched with thirst and in need, I shall give them a portion; I will be the donor and they will be the recipient.'"
Having given the gift, he made this aspiration:
"May all sentient beings cultivate merit to rescue themselves and not fall into stinginess and greed.
Taking the food to a secluded and quiet place, he set aside a portion on a clean stone to give to the various birds and beasts, also making the same aspiration as above.
When you wish to eat, you should spread out a sitting mat (niṣīdana), wash your hands, and form this thought:
"There are eighty thousand families of worms within my body; may these worms all find peace and security through this food."
"I now give this food as a gift to these insects; when I later attain the Way, I shall give the Dharma as a gift.
This is how you do not abandon sentient beings.
If you do not see yourself in dire straits, eat only two-thirds of the food to sustain your own life.
Why is this so? If a practitioner eats with excessive greed, it causes the abdomen to distend and the chest to feel constricted, thereby obstructing and hindering the practice of the Path.

If one leaves aside a single portion, the body will be light and at ease; food will be easily digested without affliction, and since there is no harm to the body, the practice of the Path will not be hindered. For these reasons, one should observe the practice of eating in measured portions.

"Sixth, after having measured one's food intake, if one drinks liquids after midday, the mind will give rise to attachment and delight, seeking various kinds of juices such as fruit juices and honey syrups; thus, one’s desire for them will never be satisfied, and one will be unable to practice wholesome dharmas with a single-minded focus.
It is like a horse that does not wear a bridle, nibbling at grass to the left and right and refusing to advance on the path."
If one is equipped with a bridle and bit, the will to eat grass is severed and one follows the whims of others; for this reason, one accepts the rule of not drinking even water after midday.
Seventh, one should enter villages to collect discarded refuse from the dust and wash it until clean, making it into rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) to cover oneself and ward off the cold and dew.
If there is the condition of fine clothing, one will pursue it in all four directions, falling into wrong livelihood.
If one obtains fine clothing from others, one develops an attachment to it;
if one does not wear it, the donor will feel resentment.

If one obtains robes from within the Saṃgha, as previously described regarding the faults of being among the Saṃgha, fine robes are a source of greedy attachment for those who have not yet attained the Path.
Due to the causes and conditions of fine robes, one may encounter the danger of bandits, or even reach the point of losing one's life.
Because there are such afflictions as these, one should accept the worn-out rag-robe (*pāṃśukūla*).

Eighth, one should have few desires and be content; as for robes, they should merely suffice to cover the body, neither too many nor too few. Laypeople keep various kinds of clothing for the sake of appearing fine, while some non-Buddhist ascetics practice austerities by going naked and without shame.
Therefore, the disciples of the Buddha should abandon the two extremes and abide in the Middle Way, receiving only the practice of the three robes.
Ninth: whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, one should cultivate two dharmas, namely, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The contemplation of impermanence and emptiness is the initial gateway to the Buddha-dharma; it enables one to cultivate weary detachment from the three realms.
In the charnel grounds, there is always the sound of lamentation and weeping; amidst the scattered corpses, one directly perceives impermanence.

Furthermore, when birds and beasts devour what has been burned by fire, it is soon extinguished; through this contemplation of corpses (*śava-anupaśyanā*), one easily attains the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*) among all phenomena.

Moreover, while dwelling in a cemetery, if one sees a corpse that is putrid, rotten, and impure, one easily attains the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), which is the primary gateway for renouncing desire.
Therefore, one should undertake the practice of dwelling in cemeteries.
"Tenth: When a practitioner has already cultivated contemplations such as impurity and impermanence, they will accomplish the task of attaining the Way.
If they have not yet attained the Way, their mind will feel great revulsion; for this reason, they should abandon that place and go beneath a tree to contemplate and seek the Way."

Furthermore, just as when the Buddha was born, attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, and entered parinirvāṇa, he was in each case beneath a tree; the practitioner, following these dharmas, should always dwell beneath trees. For such reasons as these, one should undertake the practice of sitting beneath a tree.

"Eleventh, dwelling under a tree is no different from being in half a house; it provides shade, coolness, and comfort, and one develops an attachment, thinking, 'The place where I dwell is excellent.'"
Because such outflows as these arise beneath that tree, he goes to dwell in the open air and reflects:
"There are various defects under a tree:
first, the rain leaks through, making it damp and cold."
"Second, [living in a house] involves being defiled by bird droppings and being inhabited by venomous insects.
Such faults exist there, whereas in an open space these afflictions do not occur.

In an open space, one may put on or take off clothes as one pleases with ease and joy; the moonlight shines everywhere, making the mind clear and sharp, thus facilitating entry into the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi). For these reasons, one should accept the practice of sitting in the open air."

"Twelfth, among the four modes of deportment of the body, sitting is foremost; food is easily digested and the breath is harmonized. For one seeking the Way who has not yet accomplished the great task, the thieves of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) constantly watch for an opportunity; thus, one should not lie down in repose."
Whether walking or standing, the mind is difficult to restrain and cannot remain [in focus] for long; therefore, one should undertake the practice of perpetual sitting (*nitya-prahāṇika*).
When about to sleep, one does not let the side touch the mat; this constitutes the twelfth dhūta practice.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When you practice mindfulness, bind the mind to a single point so that it does not become distracted; from this, the merit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) arises.

All ordinary worldlings, due to their inverted views, cling to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-force, following after conventional designations to give rise to various false views.”
From the very beginning, the five aggregates have been pure; they are empty and devoid of "mine" or self, neither arising nor ceasing, neither emerging nor abiding.

They are neither ordinary beings nor non-ordinary beings, neither sages nor non-sages; they are free from all names and numbers, transcending the path of language, such that even all Buddhas cannot traverse them or reach them.
“You all should now each quiet your mental conditions and contemplate the characteristics of the body with careful attention.

When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, their hearts were filled with joy; they immediately contemplated this body: the skin, blood, flesh, pus, and putrid filth; the tendons, bones, veins, marrow, fat, grease, brain, and membranes; the tears, mucus, saliva, and spittle; the liver, gallbladder, spleen, and kidneys; the heart, lungs, phlegm, and rheum; the two receptacles of the raw and the cooked; the small and large intestines; the excrement and urine; the hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, and the impurities of the bladder—these thirty-six things and the nine apertures of impurity. From the outside to the inside, and from the inside to the outside, they sought the characteristic of a self, but it was utterly unfindable.

Through unremitting diligence, he finally perceived that form and mind arise and perish from moment to moment, like flowing water or the flame of a lamp: arising, they come from nowhere; ceasing, they go nowhere; and in the present, they do not abide.
Knowing that these five aggregates have been empty and non-existent from the very beginning, they eliminate all marks and realize the wisdom of suchness, thereby becoming Arhats.
As for the Bodhisattvas, having contemplated the Dharma, they attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and fulfill the ten stages (bhūmi).
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:

"Who among you is able, during the period of the Semblance Dharma hereafter, to protect and uphold this sutra, to propagate it widely, and to cause those who seek the Buddha-way to recognize its essential subtlety?"

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the eight classes of dragon spirits and deities, having heard the Buddha’s proclamation, descended from the sky, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there are those of the three vehicles who seek the Buddha-way in secluded places, we shall provide them with protection so that no evil spirits or ghosts may disturb or harass them.
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Relying upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall, in future ages, protect and uphold this sutra so that it is not severed, and I shall provide guidance for those who practice and study it.”
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Ascetic Practices of Dhūta,' and it is also named 'Detaching from Attachment and Accumulating All Roots of Goodness. You should uphold it."
At that time, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, along with the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus ends the *Sūtra on the Twelve Dhūtas* spoken by the Buddha.
